text: I now give the floor to her excellency
Camina Johnson Smith, Minister of
Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trades of
Jamaica.
Mr. President, on behalf of the
government and people of Jamaica, I
congratulate you on your election as
president of this 81st session of the
General Assembly and assure you of
Jamaica's full support. I also commend
your predecessor, her excellency Analena
Burbach, for her stewardship of the
assembly during the historic 80th
session. and to Secretary General
Antonio Gutes, I convey Jamaica's
profound appreciation for your steadfast
leadership through a decade of
extraordinary global uncertainty.
Mr. President, your theme for this
session could hardly be more timely
because today trust is in short supply.
Wars and conflicts are devastating
communities and displacing millions.
Geopolitical tensions are deepening.
Climate change is destroying lives,
livelihoods, and decades of development
in a matter of hours. New technologies,
including artificial intelligence, are
offer extraordinary promise while
presenting risks we have not yet fully
understood.
And at the very moment when collective
action is most needed, confidence in
multilateralism itself is being tested.
Jamaica's position is clear. The
shortcomings of multilateralism cannot
be solved by abandoning multilateralism.
For small states like ours, a
rules-based international order is not
an abstract diplomatic preference. It is
fundamental to our sovereignty or
security and our development. But
neither can we safeguard multilateralism
simply by defending it. We must reform
it. We must make it more representative,
more accountable, more efficient, and
more responsive to the needs and
realities of the people it was created
to serve. That is why Jamaica has chosen
not merely to call for reform, but to
help lead it. Our permanent
representative was privileged to
co-chair with New Zealand the UNAT
initiatives informal ad hoc working
group on mandate implementation review.
That work culminated in General Assembly
Resolution 80251,
an important framework for improving how
UN mandates are created, implemented,
and reviewed. Jamaica now continues that
work alongside Norway. Our objective is
straightforward. A United Nations that
spends less time sustaining process for
its own sake and more time fulfilling
its purpose. That is the multilateralism
Jamaica believes in. Mr. President, the
selection of the next Secretary General
will be one of the most consequential
decisions before member states this
year. Jamaica proudly joins our CARACOM
family in supporting the candidacy of
her excellency Caroline Rodriguez
Burkett of the Cooperative Republic of
Guyana.
Her
candidacy also speaks to something
larger. Small states have long served
the international system as
bridgebuilders, consensus makers, and
problem solvers. We learned very early
that influence does not depend only on
size or power. It can come from
credibility, from dialogue, from
principle, and the capacity to bring
people together. These are the strengths
which our multilateral system needs now
more than ever. Mr. President, for
Jamaica, the consequences of global
challenges are not theoretical. On the
28th of October last year, Hurricane
Melissa struck our island. In a matter
of hours, the most catastrophic
hurricane in our modern history
inflicted damage and loss estimated at
of our GDP. Think about that.
In a matter of hours, more than half the
value of an entire year of national
economic output was damaged or lost. A
single event
Jamaica had prepared. Years of fiscal
discipline had allowed us to build
buffers. We had put in place disaster
risk financing including catastrophe
insurance and an independently sponsored
catastrophe bond. Those measures gave us
immediate liquidity.
But no level of prudent national
planning can fully insulate a small
developing state from a climate event of
that magnitude. And therein lies the
fundamental inequity faced by small
island developing states. We can do
everything right. In fact, Jamaica's
reforms balanced economic orthodoxy with
innovation and expanded support for the
most vulnerable. And yet, one hurricane
could erase decades of progress.
We are deeply grateful to our
international partners, our Caraccom
family, our Jamaican diaspora, and the
thousands of individuals and
organizations which stood with us during
our hour of need. Jamaica has not simply
resolved to recover. We have resolved to
rebuild better and differently. Our
resilience must not be measured by how
much suffering we can withstand. It must
be measured by how well we prepare, how
quickly we recover, how intelligently we
adapt, and whether we emerge stronger.
That is why the government of Prime
Minister Andrew Holes established the
National Reconstruction and Resilience
Authority, NAR. Its mandate is to drive
reconstruction at speed and scale, to
coordinate major infrastructure
projects, crowding investment, and
critically to embed resilience in the
Jamaica we are rebuilding. We're not
simply replacing what Melissa has
destroyed. We are building the Jamaica
that must withstand the storms of
tomorrow.
We have also submitted our updated
nationally determined contribution,
completed our long-term strategy for a
lowcarbon climate resilient future and
advanced our national adaptation plan.
But national ambition must be matched by
international action. We must revive
Climate finance must become more
accessible, affordable, and predictable.
And the international financial
architecture must finally recognize what
SIDs have so long argued. Income alone
does not and cannot measure
vulnerability.
A country does not become less
vulnerable to hurricanes and other
natural disasters because its per capita
income has crossed an arbitrary
threshold. We therefore continue to
advocate for the use of measures that go
beyond GDP, including multi-dimensional
vulnerability indices in determining
access to concessional and development
finance.
Mr. President, Jamaica brings this
message to the international community
from a position not only of
vulnerability, but one of
responsibility.
Over the past decade, we have undertaken
difficult reforms and made difficult
decisions. Our debt, which once stood at
more than 140% of GDP, was brought down
to 62% before Melissa with unemployment
then at a historic low of 3.4%.
We built macroeconomic stability,
strengthened investor confidence, and
created the fiscal space that ultimately
helped us respond to the greatest
natural disaster in our modern history.
We are proud and heartened that
notwithstanding Melissa, Jamaica's
credit ratings have either been
stabilized or upgraded, and unemployment
still stands at a relative low of 3.7%.
Those gains did not happen by accident.
They required discipline, partnership,
sacrifice, consistency, and long-term
planning. Our experience has taught us
that the strongest response to a crisis
begins long before the crisis arrives in
the choices we make, the institutions we
build, and the buffers we create.
Jamaica will continue to take
responsibility for the things within our
control. But domestic responsibility
must be matched by international
solidarity and cooperation.
Developing countries cannot reasonably
be expected to simultaneously finance
climate adaptation, modernize
infrastructure, strengthen social
protection, manage debt, absorb external
shocks, and achieve the sustainable
development goals without an
international financial system
responsive to their realities. We do not
ask to be relieved of responsibility.
We ask for an international system that
gives responsible countries the space
and support to succeed.
Mr. President, that opportunity
increasingly depends on technology.
Jamaica sees digital transformation and
responsible artificial intelligence as
powerful tools. They can enhance
productivity, innovation, and
sustainable development for our people.
Indeed, they can be an equalizing force
for the world. We must therefore not
allow AI to deepen old inequalities and
create an entirely new global divide.
Developing countries require investment
in infrastructure, skills, and capacity.
And all countries require governance
frameworks that safeguard privacy and
intellectual property, ensure data
integrity, and promote the ethical and
responsible use of emerging technologies
without stifling innovation.
The pact for the future, the global
digital compact and the Abbas provide
important foundations. Our task now as a
global community is to translate
commitments into action.
Mr. President, development also requires
peace and security for Jamaica and our
wider Caribbean region. Transnational
organized crime remains a serious
threat. Last year from this very podium,
Prime Minister Andrew Holes called for a
global war on gangs, a coordinated
international effort capable of matching
the reach, financing, and sophistication
of transnational criminal networks.
Jamaica reiterates that call today.
Illicit firearms do not manufacture
themselves in our communities. They
cross borders. Criminal money crosses
borders. Criminal networks exploit
technology and operate across borders.
Our response must therefore also cross
borders. We call for stronger
cooperation in firearms tracing and
interdiction, intelligence and
information sharing, financial
investigations and law enforcement
capacity building. We also urge major
arms enforcing exporting states to
strengthen export controls and post
delivery verification.
At home, Jamaica has invested heavily in
our security forces, strengthened
legislation, enhanced intelligence
gathering, oversight, and transformed
policing. The results are remarkable by
any standard. In 2025, Jamaica recorded
its lowest number of homicides in more
than three decades. And in 2026, with
even further reductions, the Global
Peace Index ranked Jamaica the most
peaceful country in the Caribbean. We
recognize that there remains work to be
done, but the direction is clear. And
our objective is not merely fewer
crimes. It is a durable ecosystem of
peace in which every Jamaican can feel
safe, raise a family, do business, and
fulfill his or her potential and retire
in paradise.
Mr. President, nowhere in our region is
the challenge of criminal gangs more
devastating than in our caraccom sister
nation of Haiti. Jamaica stands firmly
with the Haitian people. We urge
sustained international support for the
gang suppression force, the Haitian
National Police and its armed forces.
This support must include the financial,
logistical and operational resources
necessary to restore security. We
further call for the security council to
renew the mandate of the GSF at this
imperfect but particularly critical
juncture. We are at a crossroads. We can
either lose gains or we can build on
progress made. The international
community must send an unequivocal
message. Armed gangs cannot be allowed
to determine Haiti's future, nor that of
the region.
Security must create the space for
sustained humanitarian relief,
developmental and economic progress. But
even more foundationally, security must
create the space for political
stability, democratic governance, and
credible elections led and owned by the
Haitian people.
Mr. President, the suffering of the
Cuban people is of deep concern to
Jamaica. We encourage domestic reform
and greater integration of Cuba into the
international economic system, supported
by policies that create pathways for
progress and eliminating the dire
humanitarian crisis rather than
perpetuating isolation under the
blockade. We call for continued dialogue
and constructive engagement.
Mr. President Jamaica also remains
deeply concerned by the terrible human
cost of armed conflicts across the
world. Wherever conflict occurs, our
principles must remain consistent.
International humanitarian law must be
respected. Civilians must be protected.
International law and the charter of the
United Nations must be upheld. And
diplomacy must remain our first and most
persistent instrument for resolving
disputes. Respect for international law,
including due regard for the decisions
of the international court of justice,
is indispensable to the peaceful
international order on which small
states depend.
Mr. President, Jamaica believes that
reparatory justice is at its heart about
truth, acknowledgement, justice, repair,
compensation, development, and
reconciliation.
Jamaica not only supported the General
Assembly resolution put forward by Ghana
on March 25th of this year, but we also
delivered to Buckingham Palace a
petition framing critical questions on
the matter of reparations. The petition
has now been referred to the judicial
committee of the privy council.
Mr. President
64 years after Jamaica proudly raised
our black, green, and gold flag as
politically independent nation. We
remain cleareyed about the world around
us. We know its dangers, but we also
believe deeply in its possibilities. The
United Nations must change if it is to
remain credible. Jamaica supports the
revitalization of this general assembly,
meaningful reform of the Security
Council, and greater coherence,
efficiency, and accountability across
the United Nations system. Reform is not
an act of disloyalty to this
institution. Reform is how we preserve
it. Ultimately, however, Mr. President,
multilateral multilateralism must mean
something beyond these walls. For a
small state like Jamaica, its value is
felt when our people are safer. When
opportunity is expanded, when
vulnerability does not become a barrier
to development. When countries that have
acted responsibility are not penalized
for shocks they did not create. And when
the voice of a small nation carries the
same dignity as that of a large one.
That is why Jamaica remains committed to
this institution. Not because it is
perfect, but because we're grateful for
what it has achieved and we believe in
what it can become. Small states can
help lead that effort. Our own journey
has taught us that vulnerability need
not mean helplessness, that discipline
creates resilience,
that partnership multiplies possibility,
and that even in moments of profound
crisis, nations can choose to build
forward. So, let us restore trust
through what we do. Let us manage
transformation with purpose. Let us
bring the same seriousness to preventing
crises that we do to responding to them.
And let us never lose sight of the
simple idea on which this institution
was founded. That nations working
together can achieve what none of us can
achieve alone. That is the United
Nations Jamaica believes in. And that is
the United Nations we will continue to
work towards reforming and renewing. I
thank you.
I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs
and Foreign Trade of Jamaica.
